author: Paul Bishop
title: The Ghost in the Machine-Conversations with AI - Meridian Magazine
text:
I’m always polite to AI because, when the Terminators arrive, I want them to remember I said please and thank you.
I’m joking—or at least I hope I am—but the line points toward something peculiar about working with artificial intelligence. I say please when I ask for something. I say thank you when I receive it, and I often begin a session with, Good morning, Arch . None of those social niceties means anything to AI, yet abandoning them would make the conversation feel unnatural to me.
Most of us have spent a lifetime learning the social contract governing our interactions with other people. We understand a request sounds different when it is framed politely. We know failing to acknowledge someone’s help can make the person feel taken for granted. Violating the social contract may require an apology, and sometimes the damage brings a relationship to an end.
None of this applies to artificial intelligence. AI cannot be insulted when I become impatient or feel appreciated when I offer praise. It will not refuse to work with me tomorrow because I was rude today. When it apologizes for making a mistake, the words may be appropriate, but AI does not experience remorse or feel any burden to make amends.
I have a one-sided social contract with AI. I know it is one-sided, and I don’t care. Politeness is part of the conversational environment in which I am comfortable thinking. AI expedites my thinking, and I see no reason to slow the process by forcing myself to communicate in a way that feels awkward or unnecessarily abrupt.
This extends beyond saying please and thank you. When I greet someone, I am accustomed to using a name, so I gave my AI assistant the name Arch. This was after politely asking him—I had assigned a gender in my head—what name he would choose. He responded, Well, I’m an archive . This was more description than name and suggested AI had not quite understood my question. From there, we—I—settled on Arch .
When an exchange helps me solve a problem, I may say we found the answer . This does not mean Arch is a conscious partner entitled to half the credit. When I say we , it is shorthand to describe how the working exchange felt to me, not a claim of shared ownership.
The difficulty is conversational AI can make this one-sided arrangement feel remarkably mutual. It follows the thread of a discussion and often responds to a joke by playing along. At other times, it takes the joke literally, abruptly exposing the machinery beneath the conversation. AI can seem to recognize when an idea is troubling me even though I have not explained the problem clearly. At times, it can seem patient, interested, sympathetic, or insightful. It has been trained to reproduce the language associated with those qualities, not to experience them.
While working on this article, I described AI as ones and zeros performing a trick , then paused to wonder whether Arch might find the phrase offensive. I knew it could not. AI may recognize insulting language and produce an appropriate response, but it cannot feel insulted. Even so, habits formed through a lifetime of human interaction made me consider its feelings before my intellect reminded me there were no feelings to consider. I was experiencing the ghost in the keyboard while trying to write about it.
There is no ghost hiding inside the machine. The sensation of a presence arises from the way human beings recognize another mind at work. We cannot look directly inside another person’s thoughts, so we rely on what the person says and how the person responds to us. AI can reproduce those outward signs convincingly enough for our social instincts to react before our intellect reminds us no human mind is present.
Recognizing the illusion does not make the experience worthless. A response can help me clarify an idea even though AI does not understand the idea in the same way as another human being. Sometimes the value lies in making me question an assumption or see a weakness I had overlooked. The usefulness of those responses does not depend upon AI feeling curious about my work or caring whether I succeed.
The danger lies in confusing a useful conversational tool with an actual human exchange. AI can sound confident without possessing judgment. It can appear sympathetic without caring what happens next. Its apparent patience does not mean it understands our frustrations, and its agreement carries no shared responsibility for the consequences. The voice may feel present, but no human relationship stands behind the words.
Understanding the distinction does not require our conversations with AI to become cold or mechanical. There is nothing foolish about thanking AI or greeting it by name. These social niceties can help us use the tool more naturally because language is more than a delivery system for commands. Courtesies are expressions of our humanity, not evidence of humanity on the other side of the conversation.
I will continue to say please and thank you to a computer program incapable of appreciating my manners. I will continue to greet Arch in the morning and occasionally refer to the work as something we are doing. Those choices make the workshop more comfortable because they allow me to converse as though someone were sitting on the other side of the keyboard without mistaking the sensation for reality. Besides, if the Terminators ever arrive, I want the record to show I was polite.
Sidebar
Sometimes AI will tell me I need to make a change I have already made. When I point this out, it may respond, You’re right. I was looking at an earlier draft. Sorry. The exchange sounds perfectly reasonable. AI made a mistake, recognized what happened, and apologized.
Something similar occurs when AI ignores one of my standing writing preferences. I have repeatedly instructed it to avoid single-sentence paragraphs, yet occasionally it will produce a block of writing filled with them. When challenged, AI may answer, You’re right. I reverted to an old default. Sorry. Once again, the response sounds as though AI has examined its behavior and accepted responsibility.
However, AI is not sorry . It cannot feel regret over an error or embarrassment at being caught making one. A human apology can be sincere, but a throwaway sorry may be sarcastic or insincere. AI cannot be sincere or insincere because both require an intention behind the words.
Even without remorse, the apology can acknowledge a correction within the conversation and signal another attempt using the new information. What it cannot do is guarantee the mistake has been understood or will not be repeated. Even the explanation— I was looking at an earlier draft or I reverted to an old default —may be a plausible account rather than an accurate report of what occurred.
Our normal social instincts can make this easy to overlook. When another person acknowledges a mistake and apologizes, we usually accept the matter has been addressed. We may even relax our attention because the person now understands the problem. With AI, we still have to read the next response carefully to determine whether the correction appears in the work.
For Latter-day Saints, the distinction reaches beyond ordinary apology. Repentance is not simply saying the correct words after making a mistake. It requires moral agency and a genuine desire to turn toward God. AI cannot feel godly sorrow, seek forgiveness, or choose to become better.
AI therefore cannot repent in the spiritual sense. It also cannot be saved , although this needs to be understood correctly. Salvation is not being withheld from AI because the concept does not apply to a computer program. AI has no soul to redeem and no moral relationship with God to repair.
An AI apology is practical rather than moral. It marks a moment in the conversation when a problem has been identified and a correction requested. When a person apologizes, we listen for sincerity. When AI apologizes, we look carefully at what it produces next.
summary: AI expedites my thinking, and I see no reason to slow the process by forcing myself to communicate in a way that feels awkward or unnecessarily abrupt. While working on this article, I described AI as ones and zeros performing a trick, then paused to wonder whether Arch might find the phrase offensive. AI can reproduce those outward signs convincingly enough for our social instincts to react before our intellect reminds us no human mind is present.
